The 300 baud interface uses the lite pen interrupt to :INPUT! You
would HAVE to have it connected as recommended by Bally or "no go"!
If you INSIST on running LILL' WHITE RAM at 300 baud (and for the
life of me I can't see why, do you know how long it takes to dump out
a 16K program at 300 baud?), then I recommend BUILDING a 5VOLT
REGULATED supply (similar to the one that the 64K ram board docs
show) and run LILL' WHITE RAM from that. I used a "hommade" one of
sorts in development. The only problem is that the common DOESN'T
come out to the lite pen plug in LILL' WHITE RAM, and if you open up
the unit, the warrenty is void. You now have a choice, void the
warrenty, or tap into the common from inside the Arcade. Whatever you
do DON'T hook up BOTH LILL' WHITE RAM and the 300 baud interface from
the Arcades 5V source! If you do, you will have another dead Arcade
to put on the pile!!!

Mike W.

5505:
Adam,

I saw your post and questions on the arcade version of Gorf, and thought I
would make an attempt at answering some of them.

>  I was just browsing Ebay and I came across a Gorf PCB set. Since it is
> based on the Astrocade I always figured that it would look like the
> Seawolf II board.

I believe after Seawolf II, Midway went to a cardcage system for their
commercial Astrocade hardware. It was used in several games, including (but
not limited to) Robby Roto, Wizard of Wor and Gorf. While I am not sure, I
believe that the reasons were for reusability. For example, in all three of
the above games, four of the six cards are the same and can be swapped into
any of the games. All the cards together make up the complete game system.

> What the HECK are all these boards?

Using Gorf as an example, the cards in the cage are:

1. Game board
2. ROM/RAM board
3. Pattern Transfer Board
4. CPU Board
5. Video RAM board
6. Video RAM board

As for what is on the boards (not extensive, but just an idea):

1. Game board: This board always has the pin connectors that hook to the
harness in the game controls and output. It has two custom IO chips, which
among other things decode the inputs. I believe this board generates the
starfield. The sound and music circuitry is here as well as the speech chip
(Votrax SC-01). Video is also output from this board, which I think is a
composite signal, which is fed to a separate board that converts it to RGB
for a standard arcade monitor.

2. ROM/RAM board: Pretty much just what it says. The ROMS (or EPROMS) are on
this board which hold the game code in eight 4K (EP)ROMS for a total of 32K.
The static RAMs are also on here, which in Gorf provide 16K of workspace
RAM.

3. Pattern Transfer Board: The job of this board is to simply move blocks of
data around at a high rate of speed bypassing the processor. You basically
tell the board the from and to location, how much data to move and then say
"go!". I know it has functions to manipulate the data, which I *think* mimic
the Magic RAM functions. For example, some of the "status latches" in the
board description is direction, expand, constant, flush, flip and flop.
(Wizard of Wor manual page 50).

4. CPU board: This board has, you guessed it, the Z80 CPU. It also contains
two other custom chips, the address chip and the data chip. Their
descriptions are given on page 57 and 58 of the Wizard of Wor manual. Most
of you are familiar with the custom data chip. That's the one in the
Astrocade that gets really hot and goes out if you don't have good
ventilation. There is even a heatsink on the arcade version (if it is
missing, be sure to glue one on or your chip will usually not live too
long).

5/6. Video RAM board: These two boards work together to make 16K of video
memory (each card has 16K, but is only 4 bits wide). Due to the wiring on
the bus, the cards are identical so you don't have to worry about getting
them in the wrong order. The whole 16K is not used, there is about 64 bytes
that are not displayed and seem to be used for the stack. Just like in the
Astrocade, you can also set the memory blanking so you can use more of the
video memory as working RAM, but there is so much available RAM I can't see
a reason for doing so.

> Also, there is another auction for "Bally Gorf arcade audio amp and RGB
> interface pcb:"  ... What about the RGB Interface, is that what this
> schematic (from Tony Miller), located at Ballyalley.com  ...

The schematic on Ballyalley is the schematic for the RGB converter board
used in the arcade games (Wizard of Wor manual page 86). I forget what the
Astrocade puts out, but the cardcage in the arcade version actually puts out
some kind of composite signal (R-Y, B-Y, and VIDEO) and the RGB board
converts these signals to RGB so it can be sent to a standard (for the day)
arcade monitor.

> Does the Audio board have the speech synthesizer chip on it?

No, the audio board is just an amplifier (with volume controls) for the
speakers. The actual audio and speech is generated on the game board (seen
#1 above).

Thanks for asking these questions, Adam. It felt good to be able to answer
something on the board for once. :-)  Just don't take the above as gospel
without double checking the info... a good idea in any case.

Cheers!
-Commander Dave

5508:
Whoo-hoo! Awesome (but half-off-topic) news! I had e-mailed Don Worth
(programmer of Beneath Apple Manor) earlier this (Thurs) afternoon.
He's already replied! Unfortunately, he's pretty sure that he lost
the source code to that game, and all floppy discs, over the years.

However, he did suggest that maybe I should try to reverse-engineer
his game, to obtain the "source code" that way. I wrote back, to
pester him about it again: to make a sort of counter-offer. (He was
one of the masters of copy protection, on the Apple II, back when. He
and another guy disassembled Apple DOS and wrote a book about it, way
back in 1981. No way in heck is Lowly Lil' Me ever gonna be able to
hack through whatever other-wordly bits of arcane anti-hacker-voodoo
he put onto his OWN Apple floppy, to protect it?! But I'm sure that
HE could do it; so I offered to mail him my original BAM floppy.)

Other options: source code from other ports. He wrote the first
version on the Apple II (plus?) in 1978; and later did an improved
Apple game: with later ports or releases for both the Atari 8-bit and
the IBM PC. I'm currently of the fond hope that -- since he said or
implied that he had to disassemble his own original game's object
(compiled?) code, to make the later Apple upgrade version, that he
was religeous about keeping the source code to the two later ports?

Right now, he's sort of pleasantly amused that I remember his game so
fondly. It was one of the first major games I owned, for any 'fuser:
and in a sense put me on the path to being an old computer nerd, now.

It may have been black and white, and had crude sound, but it was a
mind meld of sorts with a talented programmer. Just hard enough and
just fair enough of a game to make you want to keep playing it; while
making you feel like you accomplished something, the more you played.
The idea of making you EARN your next "save": devilishy ingenious! I
was constantly in fear of dying before I saved up enough for
that "brain scan"! If you got killed before that, it was a real loss!

It's mostly off-topic, so I'll keep it short (for me!) ... but when
he told me that he may still have a few original sheets from the
yellow pads that he hand-wrote his original game's code on ... WOW!
You better believe I (gently?!?) told him other folks like me would
find that to be wonderful stuff to see, if he were ever to scan some
of them in, and post them for viewing or download on his home page!

 -- Ward Shrake --

5511:
Some updates, after having looked through my old C64 diskettes:


re: VIC-20 games

I can't find the darned things! That stinks!



re: "Sword of Fargoal"

I can't seem to locate the VIC-20 version; which is annoying, since I
just saw it probably a week ago. The C64 version I did locate; and I
had been doing some minor reverse-engineering work on it. The main
core of the program -- the BASIC portion -- is 74 blocks long; which
when divided by 4 to get kilobytes, comes out to 18.5k long. Ouch!
And that's not counting the redefined font / character set or any of
the machine language routines: just the main BASIC part of things.


re: Colorbot

I did find a working copy of that old Compute! type-in program; and
set it aside. It's mostly BASIC, with one major exception: an ML bit
of code that cycles or flashes the colors of certain objects, using
(as I recall it now) some interrupts, to change those colors quickly.
The game play seems a bit sluggish, but that's to be expected for an
all-BASIC game. Feels like an ML game, just to look at it, however:
as the graphics are pretty fast and flashy. I'll have to solder up a
new monitor cable, or (shudder!) use my old CBM RF box, to try the
version that John had originally written for the VIC-20 machine.


re: Hardhat Climber

I also found a working copy of this one. I hadn't mentioned it yet,
because I'd forgotten all about it. Mostly if not all BASIC; and a
bit sluggish because of it. It's loosely based on Donkey Kong, at a
glance -- the screen layout and gameplay, I mean -- but seems like it
wouldn't take much to convert the idea to a Miner 2049'r type game?


re: Lemonade

I'd also forgotten about this one. I have some copies of it, too. It
was written to work on pretty much any old Commodore system, so it
used the built-in Commodore character set rather than redefinable
characters or sprites. As I recall, from having played with its code
a bit, before, it's pretty bloated in size, compared to what you
might expect, given the type of game it is. Could be put on a diet,
if it were one of the programs on our list of possible BASIC ports.

I wasn't refering to 1.8K, but to say a 16K Viper, such as Lance or
Paul have. Goldigger was copied out of a book by Dave Carson (he
didn't come up with the concept). The Blue Ram program fits easily
into 3100 bytes (the space used by a 4K Blue Ram). The origional
program was over 10K in length and used a syntax where a simple PRINT
statement used 3x as many characters to set the parameters, not to
mention that the command PRINT uses 6 bytes as compared to the
Arcade's ONE! In the end, Dave used about 1/4 the space to accomplish
the same thing in the Arcade as the "traditional" Basic would use.

As to the machine code part, unless the other system also uses a Z80
you will see some savings here also. See if you can duplicate an LDIR
in an 8080 or 6502 and count how many bytes it takes. I'll bet it's
more than TWO! Yet I wouldn't expect to see the savings like the
Basic part of the program gets.

So then, what can be expected out of the Arcade? Only your
imagination stops you. Mike Peace got extreme speed out of a Basic
program, and Dan Dresher got an entire map of the continental US into
1.8K and made a game out of it! What can you do? You have the
advantage of possessing all of the above info, plus you have this
group where you can "put your heads together" and solve (nearly?)
insurmountable problems! As an example, I lit into The Gate Escape to
fix the problem of not starting without an 8154 and managed to do it
by borrowing 9 bytes from Mike Peace's "signature" in the 4K game,
and doing it so that the keypad overlay can, but need not be present.
I haven't started the larger version yet, but expect it to go better,
as a tape loading instruction can come out.

Finally, as I said once before: Who was it that said "if it's
possible, then it's already been done, if it's not, it will be"

5540:
Commodore's BASIC was first since the PET came out in 1977.  A version of
that Microsoft-created BASIC was in all of the PET models, the Vic-20, the
C-64, C-16/Plus/4 and C-128 (much improved in the latter two).  It was only
with the release of the Amiga that Commodore stopped using it since it was
based on a different processor class (though they still used a BASIC from
Microsoft).  They were the only company to pay Microsoft a one-time fee for
their version of BASIC used in their 8-bits and were able to use it
indefinitely.  Microsoft didn't make that mistake again.

repaired or the cart turns up at some point.

I beg to differ. As far as taking that quite literally: bytes NEVER 
stray!  :-) They stay exactly where they were originally put. They
may degrade over time -- one bit that was a zero may turn into a one,
or vice versa -- but they never "take a walk" and end up at another
memory address. It's about as possible as the sun deciding to rise in
the North, versus the East. The only way for something even remotely
like that to happen would be for someone to mess up where they put
two or more address lines. That would move entire blocks around; but
I see no chance of that happening, in this case, since 20+ other ROM

Just so that you know Ken and I are not making this up, you can
read it in the Nutting Manual.  Here is a link to the PDF version of the
manual:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/nutting_manual_project_2-1.pdf

Check out page 72 (which I'm quoting here:)


CARTRIDGE CONVENTIONS
---------------------

Two types of cartridges may be used with the Bally Professional Arcade.
The first type, called an autostart cartridge, is entered immediately
after reset.  The only initialization that is performed before entry
is the set-up of the stack pointer to point just below system RAM and
the establishment of "consumer mode" in the custom chips.  RAM is not
altered in this mode.

The second type, called a standard cartridge, is entered after a game
selection process is completed.  Considerably more initialization is
done by the system before control transfer.

            1)      System RAM is cleared to 0
            2)      The ACTINT interrupt routine is enabled
            3)      The MENU colors are set in the left color map
            4)      Vertical blank is set at line 96, horizontal
                    boundary at 41, and interrupt mode at 8.
            5)      The screen displays the menu frame.
            6)      The shifter is cleared.

An autostart cartridge is indicated by a jump instruction (opcode C3H)
at location 2000H.  This jump instruction should branch to the starting
address of the cartridge.

A standard cartridge is indicated by a sentinel byte of 55H at location
2000H.  Following this byte is the first node of the cartridge's menu
data structure.  This data structure gives the name and starting
address of each program in the cartridge.  (See MENU)


Burning the ROM to cartridge would not make it work.  If the first byte were
changed to a $55, then it MIGHT do something (depending on how bad the
dump is).

Sure, I'll make up some bullsh.... err, uh, actually, no: can't help

six different "perfectly validated, over here" copies of the program,
in the hopes that half or at least a third of them would read just as
well, over at your place. Oh, and mixing up the types, just in case.

Other people think (and sometimes tell me that) I'm nuts for saying
this, but I'm absolutely convinced that certain things HAVE to be
matched up, closely, by their era. In this case, I'm thinking those two
chips you mentioned were likely a bit older than the others I sent; and
the two older ones read fine, but the four newer ones weren't having
any of it. Which is why I'm still using an early 1980's computer and
matching reader/burner as my initial dumping system; and then using an
older PC to transfer that digital info to; and only then, a modern PC.

I don't trust computers to do what they're supposed to. And others tell
me I'm coo-coo for it, and paranoid: but my results are often better.

People who've never dumped ROMs don't understand that tons of stuff is
just not in any book, anywhere. Data books are primarily a sales tool,
to sell chips to customers. Preferably, in huge quantities. As such, a
lot of "we'd rather not mention that minor problem" stuff gets edited
out, before it goes to print. (Or at least, that's how I see it!)

Kind of like video game reviews, in magazines. My policy is: buy up any
issues that look interesting, and just file them away, without buying
any of the products they are saying you just HAVE to have, "right now"!
In a few years, when another system's profit margins are potentially a
lot higher than the now-aging system(s) they once creamed themselves
over ... at that point, and only at that point, will the mags start to
say stuff like, "While that (game or system) was great in it's time, it
is now (blah, blah, make it sound like you'll get leprosy from buying
one; and your best friend's head will catch fire, it you still have
one, tucked away somewhere, out of sight of the Gaming Fashion
Police.)" It seems they mention the good points, up front; and aren't
shy about naming the counter-balancing bad points, for several years.

I'm not sure data books ever really get to that point? I just know that
ta lot of "undocumented" things are bound to happen, in many cases. If
you trust your machinery to live up to the sales hype, you'll end up
having bad results, quite often. If, like me, you don't trust it, and
you plan for Serious Paranoid Overkill, at many steps: it helps. I may
seem at times like I treat certain things like trying to carry a well-
greased watermelon, using teflon gloves ... but usually, it works out.

Had I simply sent you one chip, and trusted that it was readable ...

5571:
I'm not sure if this is the reason that Mike is having trouble reading the EPROMs that Ward sent to him, but it might have something to do with it.  Certainly I have had trouble reading some EPROMS from Mike and I think that this may have something to do with it.

Memory chips ("standard" memory or EPROMS) are usually upgraded over the course of years.  The one upgrade that REALLY makes a difference is the access time (speed) of the chip.  Older 2732 EPROMs (just for a random example) can have write speeds as high as 450ns (maybe even higher).  If a computer requires memory of 450ns and it uses 100ns memory instead, then it doesn't care because the memory keeps up with the computer just fine.  The reverse is not true.  Slow memory used in place of faster memory simply will not work.  Sure, this may seem obvious, but datasheets found on the internet are usually for a few of the more popular brands.  Let's say you are using the a TI 2732.  Then you would, ideally, want to use the datasheet for that exact TI 2732.  You may be able to get away with using another manufacturer's datasheet but there ARE going to be differences between the chips.  You may not run into them, so it may not matter to you.  But, if you do run into them, then you may never figure-out the problem without the EXACT datasheet for the chip that you're using.

One of my electronics instructors had a saying that I have really come to like.  He said, "Every difference makes a difference."  As I learn more about electronics I learn the truth of this statement.

Hey, Everyone!

Investigating the Lemonade game got me interested in older BASIC books (which never really interested me before).  I ordered MANY used computer books at the end of last week.  Mostly these are about BASIC computer games.  I ordered all of them in "acceptable" to "good" condition from Amazon.com.  In all I've bought fifty-one books.  Here's the list of what I bought.  Following the list are some explanations of how I choose some of the books:

Dr. C. Wacko Presents Commodore 64 BASIC and the Whiz-Bang Miracle Machine
Dr. C. Wacko's Miracle Guide to Designing and Programming Your Own Atari Computer Arcade Games
Fun and Games with the Computer
Game Playing in BASIC
Games for Your Vic-20
Golden Flutes and Great Escapes: How to Write Adventure Games for the C64
How to Build Your Own Working 16-Bit Microcomputer
Mapping the Atari [Note: May not be the Revised Edition for the XL series]
Mastering the Vic-20
More BASIC Computer Games
More Than 32 BASIC Programs for the C64
Most Popular Subroutines in BASIC
Programs in BASIC for Electronic Engineers, Technicians and Experimenters
QBASIC Games & More
Science Computer Programs for Kids and Other People
Speedscript for Atari Computers
Sprites and Sound on the Commodore 64
Tim Hartnell's Giant Book of Computer Games
TV Typewriter Cookbook
Vic-20 Programmer's Reference
Vic-20 User's Guide
Vic-20: Games, Graphics and Applications


That is SOME list, isn't it?!?

While I was ordering I asked myself "Will I read most of these books?"  My answer was, "No, of course not!"  I don't even know ANYTHING about most of these books other than the titles.  However, some of these books I WILL read, cover to cover, with excitement.  Other books I will be presently surprised to find are AWESOME.  A few of these books have nothing at all to do with programming, despite their names; these are historically significant books from the mid-seventies (TV Typewriter Cookbook, for example).

During my search for computer books I learned something interesting.  Many of these books were written for more than one platform (i.e. Atari, C-64, Vic-20, etc).  Sometimes one version of the book would be $25 for one platform and ten cents for another.  Needless to say, I went with the less expensive version of the book!

These books are typically for "micro-computers."  Meaning that the BASIC programs were aimed at one type of BASIC (oftentimes Apple or TRS-80) and then there would be a chapter of conversions in the back.  Some of these books even pre-date that.  They are BASIC games for pre-1975 computer? so they were meant to run with BASIC on mainframes.  These types of games had no graphics (as they ran on a terminal), but they can be converted easily enough (I suppose) to modern computers.

Then there is the opposite end of the spectrum: books written with a certain computer in mind.  Games in BASIC (especially graphic games) written for the Atari or C64 are usually just crammed full of PEEKs and POKEs.  These could be a big pain to convert to another format.  Then again, these are also the games that look the best.  BASIC games have never been known for their speed, but static graphics could be achieved that were more than just acceptable.  Games that redefined character sets also often looked pretty good.

When I found a book by an author that seemed promising I would search for other books by the same author.  This proved VERY fruitful, and is the way that I found many of the books.  I was surprised that some authors wrote books from the early seventies well into the nineties (presuming that it isn't just another author with the same name).

Most all of these books I picked by title (and price!) alone.  I'd say that there were really no more than five or six reviews on Amazon in this whole bunch.  This surprised the heck out of me.  But then, why WOULD these books be reviewed?  Who is using them now?  No one.  The reviews of the books that I read were always written by someone that had strong ties to the book back in the day.

Some of these books I didn't buy randomly.  I had either heard of them, or there was a review of them.  Here are some of those titles that I bought KNOWING what to expect, at least to some extent.

Apple Graphics and Arcade Design - This book is by Jeff Stanton, a guy I know from California.  I've tried to find this book for YEARS, but it was always way out of my price range.  Jeff also wrote a version of this book for the Atari.  He told me once that some of the programmer's at Atari used the Atari version of the book to get them up to speed to program the Atari 5200 (since it was basically an Atari computer).

Artist and Computer - This book is available online for free at http://www.atariarchives.org/.  It was published in 1976 and looks historically fun to read.

Atari BASIC Sourcebook - This is the source code for Atari BASIC for the Atari home computers.  This book was less than a buck and it usually is FAR more.  I tried to purchase it a few years ago (for a reason I can't even remember), but I couldn't afford it.

BASIC Computer Games, More BASIC Computer Games and Big Computer Games - These three books were published by Creative Computing in the early to mid-seventies.  The first one was published in 1974, I think, and was meant for mainframes.  When BASIC became available for "micro-computers" these books were already on the shelf and ready to use.  They became bestsellers and are quite interesting to flip though (I used to own two of them).

C64: Programmer's Reference Guide - Awesome book.  If you've seen it, then you know why!

Commodore 64 User's Guide - Besides teaching BASIC, it also happens to contain the first full program that I ever typed in.  Do you remember the short program that you type in that has a hot air balloon fly across the screen with the Commodore logo on it?  I LOVED it.  It amazed the hell out of me.  Of course I had NO idea how it worked!

Computer Graphics Primer - This is another book that I've glanced through over at http://www.atariarchives.org/.  It was published in 1979.  It covers the micros of the time, but also high end computers, which I actually find more interesting since they didn't get as much coverage.  Looks like a real fun read.

Computer in Science and Social Studies - I only bought this because of the author, David H. Ahl (the founder of Creative Computing magazine).  This was published in 1983 and I actually have NO idea what it is about.  Now, that's faith in an author for you!

Computer Mathematics: A Sourcebook of Ideas - Another book by David. H. Ahl, this one published in 1980.  I dig math, as it's like some hidden language that anyone can learn, but that hardly anyone does.  It's too bad that I am severely lacking in my math skills.

Compute's Beginner's Guide to Commodore 64 Sound - One of the few Compute! Books that I was able to afford.  The C64 has absolutely the BEST sound of any 8-bit.  Not sure how much use I'll get from this book, but I'm sure it will at least prove an interesting browse.  Here's a weird side note: I searched for this book on Ebay too, but in the search I also found a circuit board that lets you add a SID to your C64.  Very strange.  I've heard of similar boards for the Atari computers that let you add an extra Pokey chip for stereo sound.

Dr. C. Wacko's Miracle Guide to Designing and Programming Your Own Atari Computer Arcade Games - This is one of the very few books that I bought because of a review on Amazon.  The review compared this to a "For Dummies" book.  I would NOT have bought this book by its title alone.

Golden Flutes and Great Escapes: How to Write Adventure Games for the C64 - I already have a version of this book for the TRS-80.  It's pretty neat.  This one is for the C64, so I picked it up for a penny.

How to Build Your Own Working 16-Bit Microcomputer - This is another non-programming book.  It's hard to find books about how to build a computer from component parts, as there are damn few of them.  I've actually already received this rather thin book that tells how to create a computer using a TI CPU (the same CPU in the TI-99/4a, I think).

Mapping the Atari - I bought this on the off-chance that this may be for the XL series too.  It probably doesn't cover them, but the version of the same book that DOES cover the XL series starts at $50.  Ouch.

QBASIC Games & More - I can't even run Q-BASIC unless I use one of my older laptops.  I can't recall seeing a book on Q-BASIC games before, but then again, I was not into the PC world at the time.  I'm quite curious how things were in the PC BASIC world circa 1993 (which seems like a rather late date for this book).

Speedscript for Atari Computers - This is an easy to use word processor published by Compute! (first in the magazine, I think).  When I gave my brother an Atari 8-bit computer to use in about 1993, I gave him this word processor.  This book has the sourcecode for it.  The book is available for several platforms.  I wanted the Atari version, and it just so happened to also be the least expensive.

TV Typewriter Cookbook - This is another historically significant book.  I owned this book in 1993 or so, but I didn't appreciate (or understand!) it at the time.  Check out the review on Amazon if you've never heard of this book.

Vic-20 Programmer's Reference and Vic-20 User's Guide - I don't know a whole lot about this system, but I do know that these books will be helpful if I try to convert a Vic-20 game to the Astrocade.  I recall reading that since this Reference Guide is written so well, Commodore used the same format for the C64 version.  Since the Vic-20 only had 3.5K available to BASIC (I think) Vic-20 programs are almost a perfect match for Astrocade BASIC.


That's a LOT of book!

Lance;

On the 64K RAM board, there were places to put switches to write
protect the 1st 8K, the 2nd 8K, and the rest. When I used this unit
back in the 80's to do screen dumps from taped cartridges I used the
on board "move" subroutine to place the program into the !2000
through !3FFF area and ran the RAM in that area like a game
cartridge. Meanwhile, Snoop Camera resided in the !6000 area
UNPROTECTED! In fact, I never even write protected the game running 
in !2000 either! What I'm saying is, that although "write protect" is
a nice feature, normally it's not really needed. However, if you were
to replace the on board ROM with one of your own and wished to test
it on the R & L board (or some hommade device) it would HAVE to be
write protected, as the "MAGIC RAM" would keep trying to write into
it for character generation. We included it on our RAM for game
cartridge testing mainly, as Ken already has said. If you find
another use for it fine. As to writing a Basic program, the author's
creed is - SAVE-SAVE-SAVE!!!

I'd certainly be interested in seeing what theories about adventure designing this author puts forth, since he wrote it back in the day itself, when Infocom was current, and this was still a relatively new genre, free of revisionist theories and somewhat overblown academia. I enjoyed Twisty Little Passages, but the parts I found most enjoyable had to do with the history of Infocom, and the quotes from game writers themselves. The author, however, is ever at pains to apply a scholarly term to every little thing. I’m even more convinced than ever that I'm correct in my view that the terms "literature"/"literary" and “non-“ are based on a fallacious distinction. The overall feeling I got was that the author was more interested in the future possibilities of interactive fiction than the reasons for which already existing games have worked so well. He seems to find mostly negative or "falling short" kinds of things to write on every title he brings up from the past. And he mentions online competitions without pointing out how pointless and detrimental it is to reduce the craft to such juvenilia.

So I'd be curious to peek at it sometime, just to get a the sense of possibility and optimism perceived when the craft was still relatively new, and the jaded scholars hadn't gotten hold of it yet. (A parallel: It was by this token that Steve Bloom's book was so much more enjoyable than J.C. Herz's.)

Finished dis-assembling "Video Storybook" as far as I'm going to take
it.  There is still a lot of Variables and Routines that are left
unidentified, but someone filled up an entire 8K ROM with some pretty
twisted code, leaving only 132 bytes at the end.  Here's what's inside:

VIDEO STORYBOOK

Sorry, no dancing monkeys (and those crawling things are turtles?) but
some other pictures and a few primitive drawing tools.  Assuming the
standard keypad - unless someone wants to make an overlay for this:


'C' does a Soft Reset, but since the "Reset" button is disabled this
doesn't do much.


Note: these Drawing routines all start and end with a press of the
trigger ...

'Up' Arrow starts drawing a Dotted Trace, or just a Point if NOT in
Multi-color mode.

'Down' Arrow starts drawing a Rubberband Line from trigger-press to
trigger-press.

'%' (Letter 'O' in MESS) does a poorly-coded Paint Bomb Fill (and might
crash the game!)

'mR' ('R' in MESS) draws a Hollow Circle from center then use Up/Down
for desired size.

'mS' ('S' in MESS) draws a Filled Circle (see Multi-Color modes for
colors available).

'cH' ('H' in MESS) draws a Hollow Rectangle from corner to corner (hard
to see it!)

'/' (Keypad - check your Num Lock) draws a Filled Rectangle (see
Multi-Color modes).


Note: Here's the Multi-Color Modes which affect the Drawing modes, such
as they are ...

'7', '8', '9', and '*' are basically the same three foreground colors
cycled thru.

'4' the default setting - Solid Red (the other two colors are NOT usable
as solids?)

'5' and '6' MORE multi-color modes, this time with Background color
stripes mixed in.


Screen Flashing Modes *** EPILEPTIC ALERT * SEIZURE WARNING *** You've
been warned ...

'-' (the one on the Keypad in MESS) Resets Colors to Red, Blue and Gold
(or Yellow.)

'1' Stops the screen flashing at whatever color combination is currently
displayed.

'2' Color Ramping cycles through the color wheel without changing the
intensity.

'3' Intensity Cycling from dark to light (none of these affect the
background color).


No provision was made to Select your own color preferences.  And next to
them ...

'+' (Keypad '+' in MESS) does a Hard Reset, Clearing the Screen like a
Power ON


Drawing MAGIC Modes (also has support for FLOP as well as FLIP! but not
hooked in) ...

'cE' ('E' in MESS) to PLOP write absolute, '0' to OR write, and '.' to
XOR write.


Finally, call these WORD Shifts initiated by the '=' key (Keypad 'Enter'
in MESS) ...

'=,C' for Fan Lines radiating to the Left of where the cursor was when
trigger pulled.

'=,Up' for Fan Lines to the Right (?), '=,Down' for Up (??), and '=,%'
to the Right.


Here are the Animated PICTURES (You have to make up your own story about
these) ...

'=,mR' to Draw 2 Birds, a Tree, 2 Deer and a Turtle (use Trigger to pick
one up)

'=,mS' to Draw 2 Houses and a Garden (watch the flowers bloom then
wither away!)

'=,cH' to Draw a Cottage, 2 Trees and 2 Kangaroos (make them 'Roos hop
in place!!)

'=,/' to Draw a Fire Station and a Fire Truck (or they came to put out
the chimney!!)

plus '=,7' to Draw a Cottage, '=,8' to Draw 7 Turtles, and '=,9' to Draw
a Kangaroo.


This should have been mentioned up top - Defaults to using Knob 1 and
Knob 3 to move ...

'=,*' to use Knobs to move Cursor (Hey, who has a SPECTRE handle to try
this out?)

'=,4', '=,5', and '=,6' affect the Knob control somehow, but no
difference is seen??


and Lastly, what's been called Keyword "GOTO " using Word Shift on a
BASIC overlay ...

'=,-' Use THIS every time to transfer Cursor control to the Player ONE
Joystick!!1!

5649:
Here's the text from the book:

COLORING BOOK      Bally

Object

  Using a light pen, players draw video images on their television.
Far more sophisticated than even Scribble, Coloring Book offers the
same kind of freehand drawing capability with much greater control of
detail.  The computer can be called upon to throw in perfect circles,
squares, lines or other markings, or to clone the art anywhere else on
the course.  Furthermore, you can tone and shade the drawings with a
remarkable 256-color palette.

  Using an inexpensive attachment artwork can be stored on an ordinary
audio cassette and played back on the tv.

Rating *****

  Coloring Book is typical of the new breed of nongames that is
transferring pastimes previously limited to pencil-and-paper to the tv
screen.  Opponents of technology claim that this is needless
development, that "old fashioned" coloring books work just fine for
children.  They do, and should continue to be used.  However, programs
like this one serve to take the "scare" out of computer technology for
young people, helping to make second nature this medium, which will
become increasingly important in their lives.


There are also reviews for Munchie, Music Maker, Quest For The Orb (I
saw the artwork for this one but didn't know it was for Astrocade) and
all the common games.

5661:
COLORING.BIN bombed out on me in v.0.123 as well so I went all the way
back to v.0.561 and it worked, so here's a:

COLORING BOOK manual

Selecting "1 - COLORING BOOK" from the menu starts off in DRAW mode.
Turning the knob on Joystick One changes the DRAWING COLOR (as shown by
the border color) to White (unless changed to another value)  when fully
turned to the left.  This is the background color, so even though the
cursor shows in red you can't actually draw anything, only erase what's
already onscreen.

Turning the knob right cycles through Green, Red, and Blue (or Color 1,
Color 2, and Color 3 if changed from the defaults).  You can draw in
those colors by moving the blinking (eXclusive-OR'ed in the same color)
cursor around using the joystick and pulling the trigger.

Turning the knob fully to the right causes the border (and anything else
in blue) to flash, and pulling the trigger then brings up the MENU in
X-OR Red on the right side of the screen.

MENU choices - select from CLEAR, LINE, FILL, COLOR, LIFE, and DRAW by
turning the knob, then pull the trigger.

CLEAR - will delete everything from the screen, and then return to the
menu.

LINE mode - will change to rubber-band line drawing mode, where each
trigger pull will set an end-point until the next trigger pull, when a
line in the selected color will be drawn.

FILL mode - does a (slow) paint bomb fill of the color selected,
bordered by any color other than the starting point.  Single pixel gaps
will allow the paint to leak through.  The very top line will not be
filled, this seems to be a bug.

COLOR - goes to a second menu where each of the four colors (as selected
by the knob) can be picked from a palette of 256.  Moving the joystick
left and right will change the color value from 0 to 31  (all the way to
the left will change to shades of gray).  Moving the joystick up will
make it darker, and down will make it lighter, from 0 to 7.

LIFE mode - is a fairly fast Forth version of John Conway's Game of
LIFE, until the area worked on becomes too large, then it slows way
down.  Occasionally, stray cells will remain behind when the bounding
box is resized.  Growth at the edges will come to a stop unnaturally
since the playfield isn't actually infinite.
Not really a color version - the wiping from generation to generation
should have been hidden by alternating the red from white to blue (and
the green from blue to white oppositely).  Since both odd and even
generations are on screen a the same time, any blinkers will appear to
be unchanging.  And since there is no way to tell whether red or green
will immediately die off, the starting seed should have been drawn to
the screen already in blue (or whatever the third color had been changed
to).
Unlike the other modes, the knob does nothing.  Pulling the trigger
(often gets missed) will return to the menu.  For more information,
Google LIFE "cellular automata".

And finally, DRAW mode - returns to the drawing screen in the default
scribbling mode.  Unlike the actual Scribbling game, there is no way to
enlarge the brush block size.

This is an earlier prototype.  I have seen a version that had SNAP and
COPY (aren't those the same thing?) added in, but not one with all the
other things promised.  And with only 328 bytes free (out of 8192) in
this binary, I doubt there ever would have been.

> How is it that you managed to get a text version of the Fox & Hounds

Well, the first thing I noticed about the 300-baud recordings is that they are made of short and long pulses. Then, I made a program that searched the Fox and Hounds wave file (the way I made the program it was "tuned" to process this record only, by now, due to sample rate, noise issues), looking for these short and long pulses, and dumped them to a file consisting of 0 and 1, representing the duration of the pulses.

After this, I wrote another program to generate a clean raw sound file from this dump, converted it to a .wav file and packed it to a .zip file. Due to the clean, repetitive nature of the regenerated audio, it was possible to achieve a ~290:1 compression, and this was the FoxandHounds.zip I sent you earlier.

Then, time passed and I made little progress into figuring out the encoding scheme (other than it seemed to use some sort of 4-pulse sequence encoding), until Adam uploaded the "300 to 2000 BAUD Loader" Z80 source to ballyalley.com. By examining it, got a picture of how it reads data. Then, I picked up that dump I made, wrote a program to translate it to the Basic character table and, surprise! It outputted a correct text dump.

Of course, the next step would be to reverse the process. I made a program to process a text file and translate it to a wave file. I made it to look for lowercase words (as bally doesn't use them) and convert it into the special characters for the reserved words (print, line, etc.) Then, I happily sent you the resulting file (the last file I sent you). As now you know, it didn't worked.

I took a look at the original Fox and Hounds recording, to try to find out what I did wrong but I wasn't able fo find a simple answer. Data is encoded in tape with a start bit, 8 data bits and a number of stop bits. I think probably this is the problem. The stop bit count varies wildly, I wasn't able to figure out a pattern. There are lines wit just a couple of stop bits at the end, and others seems to have much more. Characters representing Basic commands seems to have more trailing stop bits than alphanumeric ones, but I'm not entirely sure. Perhaps the stop bit count is used as some sort of parity checking?

Now, something occurred to me... what happens if you try to load the program I sent you the link through a 2000-baud interface, using the 300-baud to 2000-baud converter? In case I properly understood the reading scheme, it should be able to read it, despite the fact a real 300-baud interface will not. In case you doesn't have the file anymore, I think this is the link:

http://eggerland.googlepages.com/300-test.zip

Could you please check this for me?

AstroWav v2.0beta
Released January 29, 2004
By Bob Colbert

What is AstroWav?

AstroWav converts files that were created by BallyBin into .wav audio files.
that can be loaded into a Bally Astrocade.  BallyBin can create either
BINARY or BML files.  This document concentrates on the usage of AstroWav and
the construction of BML files.  Through BML files, you can write BASIC programs
or load machine language programs into the Astrocade.  The binary file format
is described first for reference.  While AstroWav can create audio files from
the binary format, it should not be used unless absolutely necessary as it may
not be supported in the future.  A binary file can be converted using BallyBin.
Refer to the BallyBin instructions for further details on converting binary
files to BML files.

Usage

   AstroWav [-b ] ([8], 16) number of bits per sample in .wav file\n";
            [-c ] ([1], 2) number of audio channels\n";
            [-f ] footer length in seconds (e.g. 2.5)\n";
            [-g ] gap length in seconds\n";
            [-h ] header length in seconds\n";
            [-k ] ([22050], 44100) sample rate\n";
            [-v ] verbosity 0-2 where 0 is silent and 2 is the most detailed\n";
                  Default = 1\n";
            [-w (.wav file name)]\n";
            (input .bin filename)\n";

The BML Format

	The following is an illustration of the valid tags that can be used in a BML
	file.

	<BALLY format=2 loadCount=n fileLength=n>
		<NAME>This is the name of the tape</NAME>
		<LOAD format=n loadNumber=n headerLength=n footerLength=n gapLength=n checkSum=0xnn>
			<DATA length=n>
				<BASIC>
					<LINE number=   1>PRINT "HELLO WORLD!"</LINE>
				</BASIC>
				<HEX address=0000>aa ab aa aa bb ae be aa ba bb ba ba be ab be bf <CHAR>................</CHAR></HEX>
			</DATA>
		</LOAD>
		<LOAD>
		.
		.
		.
		</LOAD>
	</BALLY>

	Tag Details

	<BALLY>
		This is the base tag for a BML file.  It must be the first tag in the
		file.

		Attributes
			format - The only valid value for a BML file is 2.  1 is used ofr
			         binary files.
			loadCount - The number of loads contained in the file.  Not used by
			            AstroWav, this is more for informational purposes and
						is optional.
			fileLength - Once again, this is for informational purposes and is
			             optional.

	<LOAD>
		This represents a load on the tape.  There can be 1 or more loads in
		each BML file.

		Attributes
			format - The valid values are 1 and 2.  Interleaved loads (used
			         for BASIC programs) are format 2, Contiguous loads (used
					 for DATA loads) are format 1.  This tag is required.

			loadNumber - The logical order in which this load should appear.
			             Optional.  Not used by AstroWav.

			headerLength - The number of seconds the header tone will be.
			               This is a floating point number and defaults to
						   1 second.  Optional.

			footerLength - The number of seconds the footer tone will be.
			               This is a floating point number and defaults to
						   0.25 seconds.  Optional.

			gapLength - The number of seconds the silence gap after this load
			            will be.  This is a floating point number and defaults
						to 0 seconds.  Optional.  Not populated by BallyBin if
						the value is 0.

			checkSum - Hex value that represents the checksum for the load.  If
			           the calculated checksum differs from this value, and
					   error is displayed by AstroWav and the correct checksum
					   is used to replace the wrong one.

	<DATA>
		This tag indicates that the actual data contained in the load is about
		to begin.

		Attributes:

			length - The number of bytes in this load.  This is used to
			         determine how long the load will be.  If the <BASIC> tag
					 is used and the BASIC program is longer then the value
					 of the length attribute, the length of the BASIC program
					 is used instead.  So, if you are writing a BASIC program,
					 this value can be 0 and it will still work.

	<BASIC>
		This tag indicates that the BASIC program is starting.  It has no
		attributes and must be contained by the <DATA> tag.

	<LINE>
		This tag contains a BASIC line without the line number.  It must be
		contained by the <BASIC> tag.

		Attributes:

			number - The line number.  Required.

	<HEX>
		This tag contains hex bytes seperated by spaces.  It must be contained
		by the <DATA> tag.

		Attributes:
			
			address - The relative address of the first hex byte.

	<CHAR>
		This tag contains character representations of each hex byte in the
		<HEX> tag that can be printed.  Non-printable characters are
		represented by the period (.) character.  AstroWav ignores the data in
		this tag, it is simply for human consumption and produced by BallyBin.
	
BASIC Template

The following BML can be copied and pasted into a BML file, converted with
AstroWav and loaded into AstroBasic.

<BALLY format=2 loadCount=1>
	<NAME>Hello World</NAME>
	<LOAD format=2>
		<DATA>
			<BASIC>
				<LINE number=   1>PRINT "HELLO WORLD!"</LINE>
			</BASIC>
		</DATA>
	</LOAD>
</BALLY>

--------------------

You can also use my BIN2BML.pl as a reference.

5696:
TRS-80 was indeed a play on the Z-80 chip, but was used in a less conspicous
way for branding purposes in the Color Computer line, even though none of
those used a Z-80 (CoCo 1, 2, 3, MC-10).  Those systems, along with the
Pocket Computer series focused on "Radio Shack", though the Pocket Computer
series made more use of TRS-80 in the actual name.  "Tandy" was more the
focus on the Model x series, which included the portable 100/102 and PCjr/PC
clones the 1000 series.  As far as I can recall, the only Z-80's in use were
indeed in the Model TRS-80 Model I/III/4/4P.
 
By the way, the TRS-80 Model I/III/4/4P all featured graphics (no color) and
could support sound through the cassette port or other hacks (the 4/4P had a
piezo speaker as well).  The TRS-80 Model II was unrelated to the rest of
the line.
 
I'm actually a big fan of the entire Radio Shack/Tandy line-up.  Most were
quite underrated on some levels.

5699:
RE: Homebrew games for other systems...  I try to buy them whenever
possible, particularly when noticeable effort has been put into their
creation.  Obviously the Atari 2600 and Vectrex have the most prolific
homebrew developers (the former in particular, far and away), but many, many
other systems receive lots of homebrew love, be they videogame or computer
platforms.  What's amazing is that the best homebrews - and there are
usually quite a few examples for several platforms - match or exceed the
best of what was ever available for the system in question (Bally War seems
to carry on that fine tradition, again underlying the importance of this
first modern effort), often supporting features or add-ons that were rarely,
if ever taken advantage of or used in a particular combination (for
instance, multiple controller support in the Atari 2600's Thrust+ or using
the extra sound channels in the ECS for a total of six with the
Intellivision's Space Patrol).  Wonderful stuff and to me the ultimate
expression of keeping a classic platform alive.  Nothing gets people
enthused about something like new product, particularly for systems that are
primarily designed around playing games.

I contacted Al, from Atari Age. He replied last night and gave me some advice.

Here is what it breaks down to.

1) Boxes, in quantities of 250 or more, cost $5-$6. These would be printed and assembled boxes. Lesser quantities would cost more per box and would not be assembled. He said that hand assembly of boxes is VERY time consuming.

2) Al could have the manuals printed for us.

OK, everone,
Here's MY 2 3/4 cents worth:

I like thr 2 boxes that Mike DiSalvo linked to. But if you want to be cost effective, and "nostalgic" looking, try thinking "outside the box".

Get a nice label and book cover done. (I have someone who can do that professionally and rather inexpensively.)
Put then together like the old Bally cartridges, in side a "bubble" pack except..
instead of bubble, go down to your nearest Wal-Mart type store and buy one of these vacuum sealers that they use for storing food.
This gives a "shrink wrap" type of seal. Then you could cover the top flep area with a fold over that has the name of the game, etc. on it.
Once you have all of your artwork finalized, go down to your local Kinko's, Office Max, etc. that can copy in color. Their copies are melted onto the page, so they won't run. They are very cost effective an will do the work for you. Some may even be able to do the stapling for you if needed. You can either put the cart in there with the instructions alone, or you could put them onto the package that Mike has chosen.

Now, the collector has his shrink wrap intact, the player has an easy way to open the package, and the money is spent efficiently.
Oh, but the way, when you are done shrink wrapping,  you can still use the machine to keep your food fresh.

Maybe that was 3 cents worth, that's debatable.
